blocks.p: Well, Diabolus resolved to have another bout with Mansoul all the same. “For,” he thought, “since I beat them once, I may beat them twice.” So he commanded his men to be ready at a certain hour of the night for a fresh assault, with special orders to bend all their force against Feel-gate and break into the town that way. The watchword he gave his officers and soldiers was Hell-fire. “And,” he said, “if we break in on them, as I hope we shall, with some of our force or with all, let those who break in be sure not to forget the word. Let nothing be heard in the town of Mansoul but ‘Hell-fire! Hell-fire! Hell-fire!’” The drummer was to beat without ceasing, the standard-bearers to display their colors, and the soldiers to put on what courage they could and play their parts like men.

So when night came and all was ready, the tyrant suddenly launched his assault on Feel-gate; and after struggling there a while, he threw the gate wide open. For the truth is, those gates were weak, and so were very easily made to give way. He posted his captains Torment and No-Ease there, and tried to press forward; but the Prince’s captains came down on him, and made his entrance harder than he wished. They resisted as well as they could. But three of their best and most valiant captains had been wounded, and could not do the town the service they wished; and all the rest had their hands more than full with the Doubters and the captains who followed Diabolus. So they were overpowered by force, and could not keep the enemy out of the town. Therefore the Prince’s men and their captains withdrew into the castle, the stronghold of the town. This they did partly for their own safety, partly for the town’s, and partly, or rather chiefly, to keep for Emmanuel the royal prerogative of Mansoul; for that is what the castle of Mansoul was.

So the enemy took possession of the rest of the town without much resistance; and spreading into every corner as they went, they cried out as they marched, according to the tyrant’s command, “Hell-fire! Hell-fire! Hell-fire!” so that for a while nothing could be heard throughout the town of Mansoul but the dreadful noise of “Hell-fire!” together with the roaring of Diabolus’s drum. And now the clouds hung black over Mansoul, and to all reason nothing but ruin seemed to lie ahead of it. Diabolus also quartered his soldiers in the houses of the people of Mansoul. The house of the town’s own preacher was as full of these foreign Doubters as it could hold; and so was my Lord Mayor’s, and my Lord Willbewill’s too. Indeed, where was there a corner, a cottage, a barn, or a pigsty that was not now full of these vermin? They turned the men out of their houses, and lay in their beds and sat at their tables themselves. Ah, poor Mansoul! Now you feel the fruits of sin; now you see what venom was in the flattering words of Mr. Carnal-Security! They made great havoc of whatever they laid their hands on. They set fire to the town in several places. Many young children were dashed to pieces by them, and those still unborn they destroyed in their mothers’ wombs. For how could it be otherwise? What conscience, what pity, what tenderness of heart can anyone expect at the hands of foreign Doubters? Many of the women of Mansoul, young and old, they forced, violated, and abused like beasts, so that they fainted, miscarried, and many of them died, and so lay at the head of every street and in all the back corners of the town.

And now Mansoul seemed nothing but a den of dragons, an emblem of hell, and a place of total darkness. Now Mansoul lay almost like the barren wilderness; nothing but nettles, briars, thorns, weeds, and stinking things seemed to cover its face. I told you before how these Doubters turned the men of Mansoul out of their beds; now I will add that they wounded them, mauled them, and nearly beat out the brains of many of them. Many, did I say? Yes, most, if not all of them. Mr. Conscience they wounded so badly, and his wounds festered so, that he could have no ease day or night, but lay as if continually on the rack; and if Shaddai did not rule over all, they would certainly have killed him outright. My Lord Mayor they abused so that they almost put out his eyes. And if my Lord Willbewill had not got into the castle, they meant to chop him all to pieces; for as his heart now stood, they looked on him as one of the very worst enemies that Diabolus and his crew had in Mansoul. And indeed he has shown himself a man, and you will hear more of his exploits later.

Now a man might have walked for days together in Mansoul and scarcely seen anyone in the town who looked like a godly man. Oh, the fearful state of Mansoul now! Now every corner swarmed with foreign Doubters. Red-coats and black-coats walked the town in clusters, and filled all the houses with hideous noise, empty songs, lying stories, and blasphemous talk against Shaddai and his Son. Now, too, the Diabolonians who had lurked in the walls and dens and holes of the town came out and walked openly in company with the Doubters. Indeed, they now walked the streets, haunted the houses, and showed themselves abroad more boldly than any honest inhabitant of the now woeful town.

But Diabolus and his foreign troops had no peace in Mansoul, for they were not welcomed there as the captains and forces of Emmanuel had been. The townsmen browbeat them all they could. The invaders had the use of none of Mansoul’s provisions except what they seized against the townsmen’s will: what the townsmen could hide, they hid, and what they could not, they gave up with an ill will. The poor souls would rather have had their room than their company; but for the present they were their captives, and captives for the present they had to be. Still, I say, they showed them all the dislike they could.

The captains in the castle also kept them under constant fire with their slings, to the chafing and fretting of the enemy’s minds. True, Diabolus made a great many attempts to break open the gates of the castle; but Mr. Godly-Fear had been made keeper of those gates, and he was a man of such courage, judgment, and valor that it was useless to think of doing that work, however much it was wanted, as long as there was life in him; so all Diabolus’s attempts against him came to nothing. I have sometimes wished that man had had the whole government of the town of Mansoul.

Well, this was the condition of the town of Mansoul for about two and a half years. The body of the town was the seat of war; the people of the town were driven into holes; and the glory of Mansoul was laid in the dust. What rest, then, could there be for the inhabitants, what peace could Mansoul have, and what sun could shine on it? If the enemy had lain so long outside on the plain, that alone would have starved them out. But now they were within. Now the town itself was their tent, their trench, and their fort against the castle that stood in the town. Now the town was set against the town, and served as a defense for the enemies of her strength and life. Now they used the forts and strongholds of the town to secure themselves, even until they could take, plunder, and demolish the castle. This was terrible! And yet this was now the state of the town of Mansoul.

After Mansoul had been in this sad condition as long as I have told you, and no petition to their Prince in all that time had prevailed, the elders and chief men gathered together; and after some time spent lamenting their miserable state and the judgment that had come on them, they agreed to draw up yet another petition and send it to Emmanuel for relief. But Mr. Godly-Fear stood up and said that his Lord the Prince never did and never would receive a petition about these matters from anyone unless the Lord Secretary’s hand was to it. “And this,” he said, “is why you have not prevailed all this while.” Then they said they would draw one up and get the Lord Secretary’s hand to it. But Mr. Godly-Fear answered that the Lord Secretary would not set his hand to any petition he himself had not had a hand in drawing up. “And besides,” he said, “the Prince knows my Lord Secretary’s hand from all the hands in the world, so he cannot be deceived by any pretense whatever. So my advice is that you go to my Lord and beg him to lend you his aid.” (For the Lord Secretary was still staying in the castle, where all the captains and men-at-arms were.)

So they thanked Mr. Godly-Fear heartily and took his counsel. They went to my Lord and told him why they had come: namely, that since Mansoul was in so pitiful a condition, they hoped His Highness would be pleased to undertake to draw up a petition for them to Emmanuel, the Son of the mighty Shaddai, and through him to their King, his Father.
Then the Secretary said to them, “What petition would you have me draw up for you?”

“Our Lord knows best the state and condition of the town of Mansoul,” they said, “and how we have backslidden and fallen away from the Prince. You know, too, who has come up to make war on us, and how Mansoul is now the seat of war. My Lord knows, moreover, what barbarous treatment our men, women, and children have suffered at their hands, and how our homebred Diabolonians now walk the streets of Mansoul more boldly than the townsmen dare. Let our Lord, therefore, according to the wisdom of God that is in him, draw up a petition for his poor servants to our Prince Emmanuel.”
“Well,” said the Lord Secretary, “I will draw up a petition for you, and set my hand to it.”
“But when shall we call for it at our Lord’s hands?” they said.

“You yourselves must be present when it is written,” he answered. “Yes, you must put your own desires into it. True, the hand and pen shall be mine, but the ink and paper must be yours; otherwise how can you say it is your petition? Nor do I need to petition for myself, because I have not offended.” And he added this: “No petition goes from me in my name to the Prince, and so through him to his Father, unless the people chiefly concerned in it join in it heart and soul; for that must be written into it.”

They heartily agreed, and a petition was drawn up at once. But who should carry it? That was the next question. The Secretary advised that Captain Credence should carry it, for he was a well-spoken man. So they called for him and put it to him.
“Well,” said the captain, “I gladly accept the charge; and though I am lame, I will do this business for you as quickly and as well as I can.”
The substance of the petition was this:

O our Lord and Sovereign Prince Emmanuel, the mighty, the long-suffering Prince! Grace is poured into your lips [Ps. 45:2], and to you belong mercy and forgiveness, though we have rebelled against you. [Dan. 9:9] We are no longer worthy to be called your Mansoul, nor even fit to share in common benefits; yet we beg you, and your Father through you, to put away our transgressions. We confess that you might cast us away for them; but do not do it, for your name’s sake. Let the Lord rather take occasion, from our miserable condition, to pour out his tender compassion on us. We are hemmed in on every side, Lord. Our own backslidings rebuke us; the Diabolonians within our town terrify us; and the army of the angel of the bottomless pit distresses us. Your grace can be our salvation, and we know nowhere to go but to you.

Furthermore, gracious Prince, we have weakened our captains, and they are discouraged and sick; and lately some of them have been badly worsted and beaten out of the field by the power and force of the tyrant. Yes, even those captains in whose valor we used to put the most confidence are like wounded men. Besides, Lord, our enemies are lively and strong. They vaunt and boast themselves, and threaten to divide us among themselves as plunder. They have fallen on us, too, Lord, with many thousands of Doubters, and we do not know what to do with them. They are all grim-faced and merciless, and they defy both us and you.

Our wisdom is gone, our strength is gone, because you have departed from us; and we have nothing we can call our own but sin, shame, and confusion of face for sin. Take pity on us, O Lord, take pity on us, your miserable town of Mansoul, and save us out of the hands of our enemies. Amen.

This petition, as I mentioned, was drawn up by the Lord Secretary’s hand and carried to the court by the brave and most stout-hearted Captain Credence. He carried it out at Mouth-gate (for that, as I said, was the town’s sally-port), and he went and came to Emmanuel with it. Now how word of it got out I do not know; but it certainly did, and so far as to reach the ears of Diabolus. I conclude this because the tyrant at once got hold of it and threw it in Mansoul’s face. “You rebellious and stubborn-hearted Mansoul,” he said, “I will make you leave off petitioning. Are you still petitioning? I will make you stop.” He even knew who had carried the petition to the Prince, and it made him both fear and rage.

So he ordered his drum to be beaten again, a thing Mansoul could not bear to hear; but when Diabolus will have his drum beaten, Mansoul must bear the noise. Well, the drum was beaten, and the Diabolonians were gathered together.

Then Diabolus said, “You stout Diabolonians, know that treachery has been hatched against us in the rebellious town of Mansoul. For although the town is in our possession, as you see, yet these miserable Mansoulians have dared to try it, and have been bold enough to send to the court to Emmanuel for help. I tell you this so that you will know how to deal with the wretched town from now on. Therefore, my trusty Diabolonians, I command you to distress this town of Mansoul more and more, and to vex it with your schemes: ravish their women, violate their virgins, kill their children, beat out the brains of their old men, set fire to their town, and do whatever other mischief you can. And let this be the Mansoulians’ reward from me for their desperate rebellions against me.”
This, you see, was the order; but something came between it and its execution, for as yet little more was done than raging.

Then Diabolus went straight up to the castle gates and demanded, on pain of death, that the gates be opened to him, and that he and the men who followed him be let in. Mr. Godly-Fear answered him (for he was the one who had charge of that gate) that the gate would not be opened to him, nor to the men who followed him. He said, moreover, that Mansoul, after she had suffered a while, would be made perfect, strengthened, and settled. [1 Pet. 5:10]

“Then hand over to me the men who have petitioned against me,” said Diabolus, “especially Captain Credence, who carried it to your Prince. Deliver that scoundrel into my hands, and I will leave the town.”

Then up jumped a Diabolonian whose name was Mr. Fooling, and said, “My lord makes you a fair offer. It is better for you that one man should perish than that your whole Mansoul should be undone.” [John 11:50]

But Mr. Godly-Fear answered him, “How long would Mansoul be kept out of the dungeon once she had given up her faith to Diabolus? We might as well lose the town as lose Captain Credence; for if one goes, the other must follow.” And to that Mr. Fooling said nothing.

Then my Lord Mayor answered, “You devouring tyrant, know this: we will listen to none of your words. We are resolved to resist you as long as there is a captain, a man, a sling, and a stone to throw at you left in the town of Mansoul.”

But Diabolus answered, “Do you hope, do you wait, do you look for help and deliverance? You have sent to Emmanuel, but your wickedness clings too close to your skirts to let innocent prayers come out of your lips. Do you think you will prevail and prosper in this design? You will fail in your wish, and fail in your attempts; for it is not only I who am against you, but your Emmanuel too. Yes, it is he who has sent me against you to subdue you. What, then, do you hope for? Or by what means will you escape?”

Then the Lord Mayor said, “We have sinned indeed; but that will be no help to you. For our Emmanuel has said it, and said it in great faithfulness: ‘Whoever comes to me I will never cast out.’ [John 6:37] He has also told us, our enemy, that ‘every kind of sin and blasphemy will be forgiven’ to the sons of men. [Matt. 12:31] Therefore we dare not despair, but will look for, wait for, and hope for deliverance still.”

Now by this time Captain Credence had come back from the court of Emmanuel to the castle of Mansoul, and he returned to them with a packet. Hearing of it, my Lord Mayor withdrew from the noise of the roaring tyrant, and left him to yell at the town wall or the castle gates. He came up to the captain’s lodgings, greeted him, and asked after his welfare, and what was the best news at court. But when he asked Captain Credence that, the tears stood in the captain’s eyes.

“Cheer up, my lord,” said the captain, “for all will be well in time.” And with that he first brought out his packet and laid it aside; but the Lord Mayor and the rest of the captains took that for a sign of good tidings. Now, a season of grace having come, the captain sent for all the captains and elders of the town, who were here and there in their lodgings in the castle and on guard, to let them know he had returned from the court with something in general and something in particular to tell them. So they all came up and greeted him, and asked about his journey and the best news at court; and he answered them as he had answered the Lord Mayor, that all would be well at last. Then he opened his packet, and drew out of it his several notes for those he had sent for.

The first note was for my Lord Mayor. It said that the Prince Emmanuel had taken it well that my Lord Mayor had been so true and trustworthy in his office, and in the great concerns that lay on him for the town and people of Mansoul. He also let him know that he took it well that he had been so bold for his Prince Emmanuel, and had engaged so faithfully in his cause against Diabolus. And at the close of his letter he said that he would soon receive his reward.

The second note was for the noble Lord Willbewill. It said that his Prince Emmanuel well understood how valiant and courageous he had been for his Lord’s honor, now in his absence, when his name was held in contempt by Diabolus. It said too that his Prince took it well that he had been so faithful to the town, keeping so strict a hand and eye over the Diabolonians, and so tight a rein on their necks, as they still lay lurking in their various holes in the famous town of Mansoul. It said, moreover, that he understood my lord had with his own hand done great execution on some of the chief of the rebels there, to the great discouragement of the opposing party and as a good example to the whole town of Mansoul; and that his lordship would soon have his reward.

The third was for the town’s own preacher. It said that his Prince took it well of him that he had so honestly and faithfully performed his office, and carried out the trust committed to him by his Lord, while he exhorted, rebuked, and forewarned Mansoul according to the laws of the town. It said, moreover, that he took it well of him that he had called for fasting, sackcloth, and ashes when Mansoul was in her revolt; and also that he had called for the aid of Captain Boanerges to help in so weighty a work; and that he too would soon receive his reward.

The fourth was for Mr. Godly-Fear, and in it his Lord said this: that his Lordship had observed that he was the first of all the men in Mansoul to detect Mr. Carnal-Security as the very one who, through his subtlety and cunning, had brought about for Diabolus a falling away and decay of goodness in the blessed town of Mansoul. Moreover, his Lord let him know that he still remembered his tears and mourning for the state of Mansoul. The same note also observed that his Lord had taken notice of how he exposed this Mr. Carnal-Security at Carnal-Security’s own table, among his guests, in his own house, in the midst of his merriment, even while he was seeking to complete his villainies against the town of Mansoul. Emmanuel had also taken notice that this reverend person, Mr. Godly-Fear, had stood firm at the gates of the castle against all the threats and attempts of the tyrant; and that he had put the townsmen in the way of making their petition to their Prince in such a manner that he could accept it and they might obtain an answer of peace; and that therefore he would soon receive his reward.

After all this, one more note was brought out, written to the whole town of Mansoul. From it they learned that their Lord took notice of how often they had repeated their petitions to him, and that they would see more of the fruit of such doings in time to come. Their Prince also told them in it that he took it well that their heart and mind now at last stayed fixed on him and his ways, even though Diabolus had made such inroads on them, and that neither flatteries on the one hand nor hardships on the other could make them yield to serve his cruel designs. And at the bottom of this note it was added that his Lordship had left the town of Mansoul in the hands of the Lord Secretary and under the command of Captain Credence, with these words: “See that you still submit yourselves to their government; and in due time you shall receive your reward.”

When the brave Captain Credence had delivered his notes, he withdrew to my Lord Secretary’s lodgings and spent time there in conversation with him; for the two of them were very close, and indeed knew better how things would go with Mansoul than all the rest of the townsmen put together. The Lord Secretary also loved Captain Credence dearly. Many a choice morsel was sent him from my Lord’s table, and he could enjoy a look of favor when the rest of Mansoul lay under the clouds. So, after some time spent in conversation, the captain went to his own rooms to rest. But before long my Lord sent for him again, and they greeted one another in their usual way.
Then the captain said to the Lord Secretary, “What does my Lord have to say to his servant?”

So the Lord Secretary took him aside, and after a sign or two of further favor, he said, “I have made you the Lord’s lieutenant over all the forces in Mansoul; so that from this day on, all men in Mansoul shall be at your word, and you shall be the one who leads Mansoul in and leads Mansoul out. You shall therefore manage the war, according to your place, for your Prince and for the town of Mansoul against the force and power of Diabolus; and the rest of the captains shall be at your command.”

Now the townsmen began to see what standing the captain had with the court and with the Lord Secretary; for no one before him had succeeded when sent, or brought such good news from Emmanuel as he did. So, after some lament that they had not made more use of him in their distresses, what did they do but send their own preacher to the Lord Secretary, to ask him that all they were and all they had might be put under the government, care, custody, and command of Captain Credence?

So their preacher went and did his errand, and received this answer from his Lord’s own mouth: that Captain Credence should be the chief doer in all the King’s army, against the King’s enemies, and also for the welfare of Mansoul. So he bowed to the ground and thanked his Lordship, and went back and told the townsfolk his news. But all this was done in the utmost secrecy, because the enemy still had great strength in the town. But to return to our story.
